annotations.limitations: Guideline changes at two hospitals during the study.
annotations.notes: Charted for mapping; no certainty rating in a scoping review.

annotations.keyFindings: Strand A. On surgical wards, acceptance was 81 percent with handshake rounds against 52 percent with written review; days of therapy 9 percent lower; about 3 more pharmacist hours per ward per week.
annotations.notes: Also informs strand B through the prophylaxis discussion.

annotations.keyFindings: Strand B. Surgeons declined recommendations that came after the ward round, lacked clinical context or had no clear recipient; in-person, early recommendations were easier to act on.
Strand B. In intensive care, feedback was welcome from a pharmacist who was part of the unit team at the multidisciplinary round and intrusive from outside; trainees needed consultant agreement.
Strand A. Across 142 evaluations, days of therapy were reported in 61 percent and defined daily doses in 38 percent, with differing denominators; acceptance was reported by 19 percent.
annotations.limitations: Catalogue of measures, not of effects.

annotations.keyFindings: Strand A. C. difficile fell by 18 percent after audit and feedback, concentrated where fluoroquinolones were restricted at the same time; small hospitals varied more.
Strand A. Acceptance fell from 76 to 61 percent as daily caseload rose; extending to surgical wards would need about 0.5 pharmacist FTE per 100 beds.
Strand B. Nurses described themselves as the link between the pharmacist's note and the team and felt invisible in stewardship reports.
Strand A. After funding ended, days of therapy drifted up 6 percent where the service continued and returned to baseline where it stopped; in-person rounds sustained acceptance.
A cluster randomised trial in 24 hospitals found audit and feedback reduced 30-day mortality by 15 percent.

claims.text: Introducing prospective audit and feedback on medical wards was followed by an 11 percent fall in days of therapy, with no change in C. difficile, mortality or readmission.
claims.passage: Days of therapy fell by 11 percent at introduction, with no further trend
claims.interpretation: Strand A: a modest effect on use without measured clinical change.

claims.text: On surgical wards, acceptance was 81 percent with handshake rounds and 52 percent with written review.
claims.passage: Acceptance was 81 percent with handshake rounds and 52 percent with written review.
claims.interpretation: Strand A: mode of delivery matters in surgery; it costs pharmacist hours.

claims.text: Surgeons described recommendations that arrived after the ward round, when plans were fixed, as harder to act on.
claims.passage: recommendations arriving after the ward round when plans were fixed
claims.interpretation: Strand B: timing and a named recipient shape acceptance in surgery.

claims.text: In intensive care, feedback was welcome from a pharmacist who was part of the unit team and intrusive when it came from outside.
claims.passage: Participants described feedback as welcome when delivered at the daily multidisciplinary round by a pharmacist who was part of the unit team, and as intrusive when it came from outside.
claims.interpretation: Strand B: remote written feedback may fail in intensive care.

claims.text: Recommendation acceptance fell from 76 to 61 percent as pharmacists' daily caseload rose.
claims.passage: acceptance fell from 76 to 61 percent as daily caseload rose
claims.interpretation: Strand A: extending with the same staff may lower acceptance everywhere.

claims.passage: Days of therapy were reported in 61 percent, defined daily doses in 38 percent and both in 12 percent.
claims.interpretation: Strand A must chart measures and denominators, not compare raw numbers.

synthesis: Nine retrieved records, charted at abstract level into two strands. Strand A (measured outcomes): audit and feedback reduced antimicrobial use modestly on medical wards; in surgery, acceptance and use depended on in-person delivery; acceptance fell as caseload rose; clinical outcomes rarely changed and were confounded by concurrent policies; measures and denominators vary. Strand B (experience of recommendations): surgeons and intensivists act on recommendations that arrive on time, in person and from a trusted team member; trainees defer to consultants; nurses carry recommendations to the team but are invisible in reports. As a scoping review, no certainty is assigned to either strand.
gradeRationale: Not assessed: a scoping review maps the evidence and does not rate certainty.
summary: Nine retrieved records charted into two strands; seven claims; no certainty assigned by design.
